title: A review on the taxonomy, factors associated with sound absorption and theoretical modeling of porous sound absorbing materials

findings.mechanism: More fibers are required for the same volume density, leading to higher air flow resistance and more tortuous path, increasing friction and energy dissipation.
findings.quote: The reduction in fiber diameter leads to rise in the value of the SAC (Fig. 11) because more fibers are required for the same volume density at the same thickness of the sample material.

findings.mechanism: Thicker material can absorb low frequency or higher wavelength sound more effectively.
findings.quote: Thicker the material, higher the SAC (Fig. 12) and the effective SAC is accomplished when the material thickness is one-tenth of an incident sound wavelength.

findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) in middle and high-frequency range
findings.mechanism: Energy loss increases due to increased surface friction in denser structures.
findings.quote: The sound absorption value is increased in the middle and high-frequency range due to an increase in the density (Fig. 13).

findings.antecedent: material density (less dense, more open structure)
findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) for low frequency sound (500 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Less dense and more open structures are effective for absorbing low frequency sound.
findings.quote: The low frequency (500 Hz) sound is absorbed by less dense and more open structure.

findings.antecedent: material porosity (increase in open pores volume)
findings.mechanism: Porosity allows sound to pass through and dissipate energy by friction.
findings.quote: Numerous studies [...] have shown that porosity is the essential factor in sound absorption behavior.

findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) towards higher frequency side
findings.mechanism: Increased tortuosity means longer passageways for sound, leading to more energy dissipation.
findings.quote: If the tortuosity has increased, the SAC increases monotonously towards higher frequency side (peak of SAC).

findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) at low to mid frequency (up to 1500 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Tortuosity does not significantly influence SAC at lower frequencies.
findings.quote: Although, at low to mid frequency (up to 1500 Hz), SAC is independent of tortuosity.

findings.antecedent: air flow resistivity (increase from low to high)
findings.mechanism: Optimal air flow resistance allows for effective sound energy dissipation through friction without blocking air flow entirely.
findings.quote: it is being found that the sound absorption value is highly dependent on the air flow resistivity (σ in Pa·s/m²). Its effect on SAC is shown in Fig. 17.

findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) in mid and higher frequencies
findings.mechanism: A greater density of fibers in the air gap leads to more energy loss, trapping sound longer.
findings.quote: The SAC increases in mid and higher frequencies as air gap thickness increases.

findings.antecedent: air gap thickness (decrease, or layer closer to rigid backing)
findings.mechanism: Bringing the air gap layer closer to a rigid backing reduces sound absorption performance.
findings.quote: It is also observed that the sound absorption performance decreases when the air gap layer is brought closer to the rigid backing.

findings.antecedent: thermal characteristic length (larger cells where thermal losses dominate)
findings.mechanism: Larger cells where thermal losses dominate contribute to sound energy dissipation.
findings.quote: The thermal characteristic length in Fig. 19a describes the thermal dissipation effects at medium and high frequencies [138].

findings.antecedent: viscous characteristic length (smaller cells and necks where viscous losses dominate)
findings.mechanism: Smaller cells and necks where viscous losses dominate contribute to sound energy dissipation.
findings.quote: The viscous characteristic length in Fig. 19b describes the effects of viscous dissipation at mid and high frequencies [138].

limitations: Passive SA materials are ineffective in the low-frequency range (large wavelength).
Empirical models are considered to be a simple model for fast approximation using power-law relations through best fitting of a large quantity of experimental data.
The Delany-Bazley model assumes a rigid skeleton material for large frequency range.
The real part of surface impedance of Delany-Bazley model tends to become negative at low-frequency range.
